n: Still in the temple and still addressing the leaders, Jesus tells a third parable of judgment.

f.w: spake unto them again by parables

n: God’s kingdom is like a king throwing a wedding feast for his son. Scripture often pictures the messianic age as a great banquet.
Guests had been invited in advance, as was the custom; when the feast was ready, servants went to summon them. They refuse.

f.g: bidden = invited.

n: The king patiently sends more servants: the food is prepared, the best animals cooked — come!

f.g: Fattened calves or sheep, saved for special feasts.

n: The guests shrug it off and go about their business — farm and trade. Ordinary busyness can crowd out God’s invitation.

f.g: Treated it as unimportant.
Business, trade.

n: Others go further, mistreating and killing the king’s messengers — like the tenants of the previous parable.

f.g: entreated = treated; abused them shamefully.

n: The furious king sends troops, destroys the murderers, and burns their city — often seen as foreshadowing Jerusalem’s destruction by Rome in AD 70.
The feast is ready, but the invited guests proved unworthy.
So the king sends servants to the main roads to invite everyone they find.

f.g: Literally the places where roads leave the city — crossroads.

f.w: as many as ye shall find

n: They gather everyone, “both bad and good,” and the hall is full. The gospel invitation goes out to all.
The king comes to greet the guests and notices one man not wearing wedding clothes.

f.g: Proper festive clothing; many think the host may have supplied it. It symbolizes the righteousness required of those who accept the invitation.

n: Asked how he got in without the proper garment, the man has no answer.

f.g: Literally “muzzled” — he had no excuse.

n: The man is thrown out into the darkness. Accepting the invitation isn’t enough; we must also be changed and prepared.
Many receive God’s invitation, but few respond in a way that makes them chosen.

f.w: many are called, but few are chosen

n: The Pharisees now plot to trap Jesus with his own words.

f.g: Snare him, as a hunter traps a bird.

n: They send their students along with Herodians — normally their political rivals — opening with flattering praise of Jesus’s honesty and fearlessness.

f.g: Supporters of the Herod family and its cooperation with Rome.

f.w: thou regardest not the person of men
f.g: You aren’t swayed by anyone’s rank or status.

n: The trap: should Jews pay taxes to the Roman emperor? “Yes” angers the people; “no” is treason against Rome.

f.g: A Roman poll tax paid by subjects in Judea, bitterly resented.
The Roman emperor — at this time Tiberius.

n: Jesus sees through their scheme and calls them hypocrites.

f.g: Why are you testing me?

n: He asks for the coin used to pay the tax. They hand him a denarius.

f.g: A Roman denarius, a silver coin bearing the emperor’s portrait.

n: Jesus asks whose image and inscription are on it.

f.g: Inscription. Tiberius’s denarius named him son of the divine Augustus.

n: Brilliant answer: give Caesar what bears his image, and give God what bears God’s image — ourselves.

f.w: unto God the things that are God's

n: Amazed, they have nothing to say and leave.
Next come the Sadducees, who deny any resurrection, with a question meant to make the idea look ridiculous.

f.w: which say that there is no resurrection

n: They cite the law of levirate marriage: if a man dies childless, his brother marries the widow to continue his family line.

f.w: his brother shall marry his wife

f.g: Descendants.

n: Their story: seven brothers. The first marries and dies childless, leaving his wife to the next brother.

f.g: issue = children, offspring.

n: The same thing happens through all seven brothers.

f.g: An exaggerated hypothetical meant to produce an absurd result.

n: Finally the woman dies too.

f.w: last of all the woman died also
f.g: The setup is complete.

n: Their punch line: in the resurrection, whose wife will she be?

f.g: All seven were married to her.

n: Jesus says their mistake comes from not knowing either the scriptures or God’s power.

f.g: You are wrong, you go astray.

n: Resurrected beings don’t marry the way mortals do. Latter-day Saint teaching understands this to mean marriages are not performed after this life; eternal marriage must be sealed by proper authority now.

f.w: they neither marry, nor are given in marriage

n: Now Jesus answers their real question — is there a resurrection — from the books of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted.

f.g: Concerning.

n: God told Moses “I am” (not “I was”) the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — long after they had died. They must still live to God.

f.w: I am the God of Abraham

n: The crowds are astonished by his teaching.
Hearing that the Sadducees were silenced, the Pharisees regroup.

f.g: Literally “muzzled” them.

n: One of them, an expert in the law, tests Jesus with a question.

f.g: A scribe — an expert in the law of Moses, not a courtroom attorney.

n: Which commandment is the greatest? Rabbis counted 613 commandments and debated which ones mattered most.
Jesus quotes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession: love God with your whole heart, soul, and mind.

f.w: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God

n: This is the first and greatest commandment.
The second is like it: love your neighbor as yourself. Love of God and love of others belong together.

f.w: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself

n: All of scripture hangs on these two commandments, like a door hangs on its hinges.

f.w: hang all the law and the prophets

n: Now Jesus turns the tables and asks the gathered Pharisees a question.
Whose son is the Messiah? They give the standard answer: the son of David.
Then why, inspired by the Spirit, does David call the Messiah “Lord”?

f.g: Speaking by inspiration of the Holy Ghost.

n: He quotes Psalm 110, the Old Testament passage most quoted in the New: the LORD (God) tells David’s Lord (the Messiah) to sit at his right hand.

f.w: The LORD said unto my Lord

f.g: Conquered enemies were pictured under a king’s feet.

n: A father doesn’t call his son “Lord.” The answer: the Messiah is David’s descendant and also divine, the Son of God.
No one can answer, and from then on nobody dares to question him publicly. Next, Jesus will speak out against them.

f.g: durst = dared.
